rv.q: I admire a production like Disruption, which hands a top-notch cast adult, contemporary material. (Any chance to watch Elizabeth Stanley flex her comedic muscle is a boon.) Rushing to meet headlines might always yield hasty results, but at least we can be grateful that, in its messiness, Stein seems defiantly anti-AI.
“Disruption” is, at moments, a thoughtful tribune of alarm and satire.
"Disruption" is a welcome addition to the "Speak Truth To Power" division of theatre.
Stein's tale of a silent-but-deadly algorithm plays out like a bonafide Black Mirror episode, and it's bolstered by an excellent cast of stage and screen stalwarts.
Andrew Stein's Disruption features a much stronger ensemble coping with the present specter of artificial intelligence in a tightly written thriller with taut direction by Hersh Ellis.
It wants to rattle your nerves, but it sometimes has trouble getting to the point.
But they can only do so much to spruce up a script that is simultaneously too ambitious in scope and too timid in execution.
Sadly, it only takes a little over two hours to not fulfill its promise of shaking our beings to the core.
Though it centers on trailblazing (and rather threatening) technology, Disruption is a pretty by-the-numbers play.
But does something persuasive result from all the highbrow cogitating? Not necessarily.
Though the future it casts is bleak, this cautionary tale is strong.
The cast is superb with no weak link in this ensemble piece.
But ultimately, there's not much more disruptive than rich, unhappy married people doing rich, unhappy, married-people-y things.
Disruption touches on some timely themes about the ways that technology is reshaping our lives, but too often the aura of intelligence here feels entirely artificial.

The latest to offer its take on the future of AI technology is Andrew Stein’s engrossing Disruption, making its American premiere at the Pershing Square Signature Center following its 2023 debut in London.
When it comes to character development, however, Stein’s writing proves more binary than multifaceted.

cn.t: A timely AI thriller with a knockout cast led by John David Washington, but critics find the tech commentary already feeling dated and the predictable plot fails to fully deliver on its disruptive promise.

vr.q: I was underwhelmed by how predictable this play was, but I was more disappointed by its immense amount of exposition over progression.
